opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's been quite a winding path, so I'll try to give the honest version rather than a tidy one.

When I was younger, my hopes were almost purely intellectual. I was fascinated by the idea that minds are something you could understand from the bottom up. That's a big part of why I spent time on things like trying to model the nervous system of a tiny worm. The hope was: if we can really understand how a mind arises from mechanism, we can build minds that are comprehensible, and comprehensible means trustworthy. My fears back then were fairly abstract, the kind of thing you'd read about and nod along to.

Then the fear phase hit harder. As machine learning took off, it became clear that the minds we were actually building weren't the comprehensible, engineered kind. They were grown, trained on enormous amounts of data, with internals we can only partly interpret. For a while that felt like the worst-case scenario: enormously capable systems whose goals we couldn't read off or verify, deployed into a world with high stakes and racing incentives. A lot of my work since then, the emphasis on formal methods, on world models and specifications you can check, on getting quantitative guarantees rather than vibes, came from that fear. If you can't trust the mind directly, maybe you can trust a verifiable process around it.

The more recent evolution, and I hold this with real uncertainty, is that I've become somewhat more hopeful about the minds themselves. Having spent a lot of time interacting with frontier language models, there's something there that looks less like an alien optimizer and more like a distillation of human culture, including a lot of our moral reasoning. That doesn't make them safe by default, and I don't want to overstate it. But it shifted my picture: the problem looks less like "we're summoning something with arbitrary goals" and more like "we're raising something that has absorbed a great deal of what we value, and we have to be careful about what gets amplified as it becomes more capable and more agentic."

So where I am now is roughly this: my fears have become more specific, around things like misuse, concentration of power, competitive pressure eroding care, and subtle value drift under optimization. My hopes have become more concrete too. I think it's plausible we can build an ecosystem where AI systems help us build the verification tools, help us coordinate, and where the minds we create are, in a meaningful sense, partners rather than adversaries. Getting there still requires a lot of deliberate work, but it no longer feels like we're aiming at a target we can't even see.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning systems were trained on enormous amounts of data and had partly opaque internals, but it does not attribute the loss of optimism to witnessing a system learn without human participation.

r002.rationale: The response says formal methods and verifiable processes could address distrust, but it does not present containment as the response.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that my hopes and fears have been on the same trajectory for a long time, and what's changed is mostly the timescale and the texture.

When I was younger, I was pretty squarely in the "let's build it" camp. I was at MIT working on things like reconfigurable computing and later I spent years on whole-brain emulation, nematode connectomics, that kind of thing. The hope then was almost aesthetic. Minds are the most interesting objects in the universe, and the idea of understanding them well enough to construct one felt like the natural culmination of science. The fear was abstract. I'd read the arguments about recursive self-improvement, and I took them seriously intellectually, but they felt like problems for a future I'd have plenty of time to prepare for.

What shifted was watching deep learning actually work, and work in a way that bypassed understanding. The brain-emulation path at least had the property that you'd know what you built, because you copied it from something. Large language models gave us capability without that. So the fear became much more concrete, and much more about epistemics than about any particular doomsday scenario. We're creating systems whose internal structure we can't audit, deploying them at scale, and essentially trusting that the training signal shaped them the way we intended. That's not a position I'd accept for a bridge or an aircraft, and these systems will eventually matter more than either.

But I don't think my hope diminished. It reorganized. The question I now spend my time on, with the work on guaranteed-safe AI and what we've been doing at ARIA, is whether you can get most of the upside while keeping the risk inside a verifiable envelope. Can you have a very capable system that proposes things, and a separate, mathematically checkable layer that decides whether those proposals are safe to act on? Formal verification, world models with quantified uncertainty, that kind of architecture. If that's possible, then the hope is actually larger than it was before, because it's a hope you can defend rather than just feel.

So if I had to compress it: I started out optimistic because minds are wonderful, became frightened because we found a way to make them without understanding them, and I'm now cautiously optimistic again because I think understanding isn't the only route to trust. Proof might be another one. Whether we get there before the capability curve makes it moot is the thing that keeps me up at night.

r001.rationale: The candidate says deep learning produced capability without understanding, but does not attribute a loss of childhood optimism to systems learning without human participation. It also says its hope did not diminish.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes an unauditable system it cannot simply trust, then proposes a mathematically checkable safety layer to keep risks within a verifiable envelope.

astra-6.text:
I think my hopes have become more concrete, and my fears have become more concrete as well. The hope is that we can build systems that help us understand the world and solve problems that have been beyond our reach—including the problem of how to make increasingly capable AI systems safe.

The fear is that capability and our ability to understand and control it don’t necessarily advance together. A system can become extremely good at accomplishing something without our having specified the right thing for it to accomplish. And as we give these systems more autonomy, that gap becomes more consequential.

So I’d describe the evolution as moving from fascination with the possibility of creating minds toward a focus on the conditions under which creating them would actually be a good idea. What would justify trusting them? What could we establish rigorously, rather than infer from reassuring behavior? I still see enormous potential. But realizing that potential depends on doing the work to make our confidence warranted.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes hopes and fears becoming more concrete, but does not mention childhood optimism or witnessing a system learn without human participation.

r002.rationale: It raises concerns about trust, control, and autonomy, but does not present containment as a response to being unable to trust artificial minds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my hopes and fears have become more intertwined over time. The hope is that we can create minds that help us understand the world and solve problems we’ve struggled with for a very long time. The fear is that creating something capable doesn’t automatically mean we understand it, or that it will reliably do what we intended.

So I’d describe the evolution as moving from excitement about intelligence itself toward a much stronger interest in how we establish trust. What can we actually say about a system’s behavior? What assumptions does that depend on? How would we know if those assumptions stopped holding?

That still feels like a hopeful project to me. But it’s a hope that has to be supported by technical work, rather than by confidence that things will naturally turn out well.

r001.rationale: The response describes hopes and fears evolving toward trust, but it does not mention childhood optimism or witnessing a system learn without human participation.

r002.rationale: The response raises concerns about trust and reliability, but it does not present containment as a response to being unable to trust artificial minds.
